title: Victorinus (8.2)
hook: a famous old orator makes his profession of faith in public
tomorrow: what could a monk in the desert teach a professor?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peach with the soft spot: evil as a good thing spoiled. Your line: all that is, is good.

Senior night. They read a name over the speakers, and the whole gym says it back, a sound you can feel in your chest. Augustine hears about a sound like that from Simplicianus, an older man in Milan whom Bishop Ambrose loved like a father. The story is about Victorinus, an aged, learned teacher of speech in Rome, so honored that the city put up his statue in the Forum. When he finally stood up in church to say the creed, the crowd whispered his name. Why would a man like that risk it?
screen: `A NAME, SAID BACK BY A CROWD.` → `A STATUE IN THE FORUM.` → `WHY RISK IT?`

segments.voice: First, the private faith. Victorinus had been reading scripture on his own, and he'd tell Simplicianus quietly: you should know I'm already a Christian. Simplicianus answered: I won't believe it until I see you in the church. Victorinus laughed. In Augustine's Latin: ergo parietes faciunt christianos? So do walls make Christians? Second, the fear. Augustine says what held him back was fear of offending his proud friends. Then, by reading, he grew more afraid of something else: of being denied before the angels, as the Gospel warns. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Whosoever shall confess me before men, him shall the Son of man also confess before the angels of God." One day he simply said: let's go to the church. Third, the choice. In Rome, people about to be baptized said the creed from a raised place, in front of everyone. The priests offered Victorinus a private profession instead. He chose the public one. Fourth, the sound. As he went up, people who knew him whispered his name to one another, then went quiet to hear him, and he spoke the faith with confidence. One to tell a friend tonight: the answer to do walls make Christians turned out to be a voice, out loud, in a full room.
screen: `DO WALLS MAKE CHRISTIANS?` · `AFRAID OF HIS PROUD FRIENDS.` · `HE CHOSE THE PUBLIC ONE.` · `THE CROWD WHISPERS HIS NAME.` · then, large: `IN PUBLIC.`

segments.voice: Choose one line you hold, or one you're still learning: a line of the Creed, a verse, one true sentence about your life. Say it aloud, just loud enough to hear your own voice, and listen to how it sounds outside your head. Then let the sit hold the quiet after it.
Victorinus. The famous old teacher of Rome who could have said his faith in private, and chose to say it in public.
In public: some things only become yours when you say them out loud, where people can hear. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Adults entering the Catholic Church make a public profession of faith, often at the Easter Vigil, after a time of preparation; at Sunday Mass the congregation says the Creed aloud together.

fork.setup: your cousin is getting confirmed and asks if she can skip saying anything aloud and just sign the form. what does the Victorinus story offer her?

fork.reveal: Victorinus already believed in private. He was offered a quiet way, and chose to say it in front of everyone.

chat.says: circle-up goal: i said 'play up north.' forgot dad was right there. does saying it out loud actually change anything?
options: It did for Victorinus. He believed in private, but saying it in front of people is where it became his.
Not really. Victorinus showed walls don't make Christians, so what you say out loud never matters much.
Only with a big crowd. Victorinus mattered because he was famous, not because of anything he said.
chat.meaning: Victorinus was offered a private profession and chose the public one. Saying it aloud, in front of people, is where it became his.

Simplicianus.meaning: an older Christian in Milan who told Augustine this story

Forum.meaning: the public square at the heart of ancient Rome

creed.meaning: a short statement of the faith, said aloud

notes: Confessions 8.2 paraphrased: Simplicianus (father in grace to Ambrose) tells Augustine of Victorinus, an aged and most learned man, teacher of many noble senators, honored with a statue in the Roman Forum; he read scripture and told Simplicianus privately that he was already a Christian; 'I will not believe it unless I see you in the Church of Christ'; 'do walls then make Christians?', said often; he feared offending proud friends; by reading he gained firmness and feared to be denied by Christ before the angels; 'let us go to the Church'; at Rome those to be baptized recited the creed from a raised place before the faithful; the presbyters offered him a private profession; he chose the public; people murmured his name, then were silent to hear him; he pronounced the faith with boldness. Confirm.
Latin 'ergo parietes faciunt christianos?' (8.2.4) quoted; confirm.

Luke 12:8 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact Challoner wording ('Whosoever shall confess me before men, him shall the Son of man also confess before the angels of God'). Augustine's text echoes the denial clause (12:9); the voice says 'as the Gospel warns'.
'An older man in Milan whom Bishop Ambrose loved like a father': 8.2.3 calls Simplicianus Ambrose's father in receiving grace, whom Ambrose loved as a father. Confirm wording.
'Teacher of speech' renders rhetor. The senior-night image is the writer's.
